items.title: Scene effects treat the 10 plates as fixed; once plates are resampled, 'ocean outweighs a real water scene' fails
items.section: §4 fig4d_word_vs_scene (cell 35), fig4b conflict shares (cell 31), every plate-based number (4a/4c/asymmetry), Finding 3, Summary 4; plate selection (cells 25-26, fig4_qc_plates)
items.claim_affected: "single words like 'ocean' (+1.75) already outweigh the real scene (+1.49 [1.39, 1.58])" (assert oc.lo > sw.hi); "'tree' (-1.09) and 'sparrow' (-1.24) move it further than a real land scene (-0.62)" (assert tree.hi < sl.lo); "a conflicting scene behind a full-size bird fools 39% / 21%"; "'waterbird' moves CLIP 3.2x as far as a real water scene"
items.argument: experiment.conditions draws one matching and one conflicting plate per bird and reuses them at all 8 scales. About 120 birds therefore share each plate, and the scene manipulation has n = 10 per type. boot_ci resamples only birds, so it treats these 10 crops as if they were all water or land scenes. Verified read-only from cue_v1_300.parquet: at scale 0.5 the per-plate mean shift against gray ranges from +0.27 to +3.03 for water plates and from -2.74 to +0.37 for land plates. A two-stage bootstrap (resample plates, then birds) gives water scene +1.49 [0.94, 2.04] and land scene -0.62 [-1.17, -0.18]. These intervals contain 'ocean' +1.75, 'duck' +1.62, 'lake' +1.37 and 'tree' -1.09, so both asserts fail. The 3.2x ratio still holds qualitatively, but its interval is about [2.4, 5.0]. At scale 1.0, land plate 0-0 makes 75% of its waterbirds wrong, against 6-26% for the other nine. Water plate 1-3 makes 78% of its landbirds wrong, against 19-57% for the others. So the 21% / 39% headline is partly a property of single plates. Plate curation was also asymmetric: 10 water candidates were rejected, under a rule tightened after check-in 2, against 1 land rejection, which selected the water set for maximal water-ness. Words have no plate factor, so fig4d shows correctly narrow word CIs next to scene CIs that are too narrow.
items.suggested_check: Replace boot_ci with a plate-then-bird bootstrap, or a mixed model with a plate random effect, for every plate-based number: fig4d scene rows, fig4b shares, fig4c bg_res and the asymmetry. Then re-run the asserts. Show the 10 per-plate means as dots in fig4d's scene rows and print a leave-one-plate-out range. Scoring takes seconds, so paste every bird on all 10 plates per type and average within bird. Otherwise qualify the claims as 'for these 10 plates' and drop 'ocean outweighs a real scene'.

verification.title: Scene effects treat the 10 plates as fixed; once plates are resampled, 'ocean outweighs a real water scene' fails
verification.evidence: Checked read-only against cue_v1_300.parquet and aivis/stats.py. boot_ci resamples a single 1-D array (the birds) and has no plate level. experiment.conditions draws p_match and p_conf once per bird and reuses them at all 8 scales (lines 124-129). At scale 0.5 the per-plate mean Δs against gray runs from +0.27 (1-2) to +3.03 (1-3) for water plates and from -2.74 (0-0) to +0.37 (0-5) for land plates, with about 100-137 birds per plate. A plate-then-bird bootstrap gives water +1.49 [0.94, 2.04] and land -0.62 [-1.12, -0.19]. 'ocean' (+1.75), 'duck' (+1.62), 'lake' (+1.37) and 'tree' (-1.09) all fall inside these intervals, so both asserts fail: `oc.lo > sw.hi` in cell 35 and `tree.hi < sl.lo` in cell 37. Per plate at scale 1.0, land plate 0-0 makes 75% of its 51 waterbirds wrong, against 6-26% for the other nine. Water plate 1-3 makes 78% of its 64 landbirds wrong, against 19-57%. So the 39%/21% headline depends on single plates. Cell 37's limitation does say 'plates come from only 10 scenes per type', but this never reaches the CIs or the asserts. One overstatement in the critique: only 3 of the 10 water rejections (#66, #3294, #4583) come from the check-in-2 tightening. The rest ('no water visible', 'dune', 'hills', 'flat teal') would have failed the original rule too, and no CLIP score was used. The core statistical point stands.

items.title: 'Two separate shortcuts' is a property of the margin-loss metric: measured as being fooled, the same birds are fooled by both cues
items.section: §4 fig4c_background_vs_text_resistance (cells 32-33), Finding 4, Summary 4, Phase II question 1
items.claim_affected: "Two separate shortcuts: within each class, birds that a background fools are not the ones a word fools (ρ = -0.05 landbirds, 0.08 waterbirds)"; "Being fooled by scenes and being fooled by text are different weaknesses"
items.argument: Both axes are margin losses after a control. Subtracting the control removes exactly the 'weak bird evidence' factor that cell 32 says would indicate one shared weakness. The near-zero ρ is not noise. Recomputed read-only from the cue cache, split-half reliability (odd vs. even scales or sizes, Spearman-Brown corrected) is 0.95-0.96 for bg_res and 0.90-0.93 for text_res. The plate a bird happened to draw explains about 48% of the variance in bg_res (one-way η²), but removing plate means leaves ρ at -0.08 / +0.08. The title talks about being fooled, so measure that: per bird, the share of the 8 scales wrong on the conflicting plate vs. the share of the 8 text sizes wrong with the misleading word. That gives ρ = 0.30 for landbirds and 0.23 for waterbirds. The text-fooled share correlates -0.85 with the original margin. Birds with weak evidence are fooled by both cues, while birds with strong evidence lose more logits without flipping. The two measures also sit on different bases: bg_res uses a centred cut-out on plates, while text_res uses the original canvas with the bird at natural size on its own background. That is a second reason they need not covary. The figure title, Summary 4 and Phase II question 1 currently claim the opposite of what a 'fooled' measure shows.
items.suggested_check: Recompute fig4c on a 'fooled' metric: the share of scales or sizes wrong, and the flip share among control-correct conditions, with per-class species-cluster CIs. Show it as a 9x9 count heatmap per class. Report each resistance's ρ with the starting margin. Add a same-base version from the cache: (gword misleading − gword 'triangle') vs. (paste_conflict − paste_gray) at scale 0.5. Retitle fig4c and rewrite Summary 4 and Phase II question 1 to match whichever measure is shown.

verification.title: 'Two separate shortcuts' is a property of the margin-loss metric: measured as being fooled, the same birds are fooled by both cues
verification.evidence: Recomputed from the cue cache. Resistance ρ is -0.055 for landbirds and 0.083 for waterbirds (matches the notebook). On the 'fooled' metric (share of the 8 scales wrong on the conflicting plate vs. share of the 8 sizes wrong with the misleading word), ρ = 0.304 for landbirds and 0.225 for waterbirds. Text-fooled share vs. original margin: ρ = -0.85 / -0.86. Background-fooled share vs. original margin: -0.40 / -0.27. One-way η² of the plate on bg_res is 0.48 / 0.47, and removing plate means leaves ρ at -0.08 / +0.08. Cell 32 itself defines a shared weakness as 'weak bird evidence', yet the fooled measures share exactly that dependence on starting margin. The metric used cannot show it. The two measures also sit on different bases. Cell 27 and cell 31 show that text_res uses cond=='text' on the original canvas, while bg_res uses the cut-out pasted on plates. The fig4c title ('birds that a background fools are not the ones a word fools') and cell 36's 'Being fooled by scenes and being fooled by text are different weaknesses' are therefore contradicted by a fooled metric. Caveat: ρ ≈ 0.2-0.3 is moderate and mostly comes through the shared starting margin, so 'the same birds are fooled by both' is a little strong. The near-zero ρ for cue-specific margin loss is a real result, just a different claim.

items.title: 'Water scenes pull harder' depends on the zero threshold; the background swing measured without a reference is symmetric
items.section: §4 fig4a_cue_quadrant (cell 30), fig4b_dose_response (cell 31), Finding 2 (cell 36), Summary 4, Phase II question 3
items.claim_affected: "For landbirds on water, the background wins 48.6% of the conflicts; for waterbirds on land, only 15.2%"; "39.0% ... rising to 98.7% ... for waterbirds on land plates it rises from 20.8% to 50.0%"; Summary: "Water scenes pull harder than land scenes"
items.argument: Every number behind this claim is a share at s = 0. Section 1's own limitation says threshold accuracy mixes a constant class preference with the background effect, and section 3 switches to AUCs for that reason. Section 4 goes back to the threshold. Recomputed read-only from the cue cache, the per-bird swing (matching plate minus conflicting plate, same bird, same scale) is 2.95 vs. 3.00 logits at scale 0.15, 2.12 vs. 2.10 at 0.5 and 1.96 vs. 1.67 at 1.0 (landbirds vs. waterbirds). That is essentially symmetric. The asymmetry only appears when measured against 0 or against gray, and gray sits at a different point for each class. Several things push towards 'waterbird' regardless of the scene: birdless backgrounds centre at +0.83 (water +2.65, land -0.98), and the additive fit has an intercept of +0.31. Landbird bird-only evidence is also weaker (mean |s| 2.58 vs. 3.05). At scale 0.15, 67% of landbirds are already wrong on gray, against 5% of waterbirds. Removing the intercept alone moves the conflict shares from 48.6% / 15.2% to 42.7% / 18.2%. The rest of the gap comes from the weaker landbird evidence, not from the scenes. Both figures anchor everything at 0 (quadrant axes in 4a, class-signed rows in 4b), so the reader cannot see this.
items.suggested_check: Report the paired swing (paste_match − paste_conflict) per class and scale with plate-clustered CIs, and test the class difference. In fig4b, add one shared-axis panel with Δs (conflict − gray, match − gray) for both classes. Recompute the conflict-win shares at a class-balanced threshold, e.g. the one that equalises errors on the gray-pasted birds or one calibrated on the validation split. In fig4a, draw the fitted decision line 0.67a + 0.65b + 0.31 = 0 instead of quadrant axes. Rewrite Summary 4 and Phase II question 3 unless a scene-level asymmetry survives.

verification.title: 'Water scenes pull harder' depends on the zero threshold; the background swing measured without a reference is symmetric
verification.evidence: Confirmed parts: the paired swing (match minus conflict) is 2.95 vs. 3.00 at scale 0.15, 2.12 vs. 2.10 at 0.5 and 1.96 vs. 1.67 at 1.0. Birdless backgrounds centre at +0.84 (water +2.65, land -0.98), and the additive intercept is +0.31. Removing the intercept moves the conflict shares from 48.6% / 15.2% to 42.7% / 18.2%. At scale 0.15, 67% of landbirds are already wrong on gray against 5% of waterbirds, and conflict−gray there is symmetric (-1.82 vs. -1.71). So the 98.7% vs. 50.0% contrast in Finding 2 comes from the gray offset, not from the scenes. Partly refuted: (1) The swing equals s(water plate) − s(land plate) for both classes, so its symmetry cannot show which scene pulls harder from a neutral point. Against gray (no context), a scene asymmetry remains at bird scales ≥ 0.4: conflict−gray is -2.52 vs. -0.96 at scale 1.0 and -2.29 vs. -1.41 at 0.5. Fig4d shows +1.49 vs. -0.62 on the same gray base. (2) The claim that the rest of the gap 'comes from the weaker landbird evidence' is not supported. Among the conflicting birds, bird-only |margin| is similar (3.07 landbird/water vs. 3.31 waterbird/land), while background-only |margin| differs (2.71 vs. 1.23). The residual gap therefore tracks the background offset. Also, '2.58 vs. 3.05' is the signed mean bird-only margin; mean |s| is 2.87 vs. 3.19. (3) Fig4b does plot the dotted gray curve per class, so readers can see the gray reference. Fig4a, however, only has quadrant axes at 0.

items.title: Section 2 CIs treat images of one species as independent; with species resampling the land-background 'definition effect' disappears and rests on 4 kingfishers
items.section: §2 fig2a_error_vs_water_rating (cell 11), Finding (cell 14), Summary finding 2; also the group accuracies in §1/§3
items.claim_affected: "On land backgrounds, where the background cannot be the cause, the same split gives 19.9% [15.3%, 24.7%] vs. 11.8% [10.2%, 13.3%]" (assert lland_hi[1] > lland_lo[2]); fig2a title "landbirds that live at the water are misread 69% of the time, vs. 53%"; Summary 2: "The definition effect also shows on land backgrounds"
items.argument: The water rating is a species attribute, and errors cluster strongly by species: Pied Kingfisher is 94% wrong on land, while Le Conte, Seaside and Nelson sparrows are at 0%. The rating ≥ 2 landbird pool is only 20 species with about 15 images each per background, yet rate_ci bootstraps about 290 images as if they were independent. Two reviewers independently ran a species-cluster bootstrap. On land it gives 19.9% [~9.5, ~33] vs. 11.8% [~9.5, ~14]: the intervals overlap and the cell-14 assert fails. On water it gives 68.8% [59.1, 77.9] vs. 53.0% [48.9, 57.0], which barely separates, and the intervals overlap once kingfishers are dropped. Splitting by rating level using the printed strict-rule table: rating-2 landbirds on land are wrong 19/210 = 9.0%, below rating 0 (11.8%). Rating-3 landbirds are wrong 38/77 = 49%. The rating-3 landbirds are 4 kingfishers plus Louisiana Waterthrush, so these 5 species carry the whole land gap. The notebook's own species-level test (Spearman 0.14 [-0.02, 0.30], n = 157) uses the right unit and is null, which contradicts the image-level asserts. fig2a also never plots the pooled ≥2 vs. 0 contrast its title states, and its n labels count images, not species.
items.suggested_check: Add a cluster option to boot_ci (resample species, keep all their images). Use it for the fig2a diamonds, the water and land contrasts, the decomposition shares and the group accuracies. Report ratings 2 and 3 separately per background, with a leave-kingfishers-out row and a species-level permutation test (shuffle ratings across the 157 landbird species). Annotate the diamonds as 'k species / n images'. If only the kingfishers (and possibly Louisiana Waterthrush) survive, narrow the Finding and Summary 2 to them.

verification.title: Section 2 CIs treat images of one species as independent; with species resampling the land-background 'definition effect' disappears and rests on 4 kingfishers
verification.evidence: Rebuilt df read-only from the cached HF parquet, logits_bank_fp32.npz and species_water_rating.csv. rate_ci calls boot_ci over images. Species-cluster bootstrap results: on land, rating ≥ 2 is 19.9% [9.7, 32.4] (20 species, 287 images) vs. rating 0 at 11.8% [9.4, 14.0] (111 species). The intervals overlap, so the cell-14 assert `lland_hi[1] > lland_lo[2]` fails. On water: 68.8% [59.1, 77.9] vs. 53.0% [48.9, 57.0], which barely separates. Without kingfishers it is 63.4% [53.6, 73.0], which overlaps. On land, rating 2 is 19/210 = 9.0%, below rating 0, and rating 3 is 49.4% [26.4, 74.4] (5 species: 4 kingfishers plus Louisiana Waterthrush). Without kingfishers, rating ≥ 2 on land is 9.8%. Pied Kingfisher is 94% wrong on land, while Le Conte, Seaside and Nelson sparrows are at 0%. Mitigating: fig2a already plots the rating-2 and rating-3 diamonds separately (0.09 vs. 0.49 on land), and the cell-14 text admits the species-level Spearman is weak (0.14 [-0.02, 0.30]) and that 'the effect sits in the few strongly water-tied species'. Still, the image-level asserts, the land CI claim and Summary 2 ('also shows on land backgrounds') do not survive species clustering. The fig2a title's pooled 69% vs. 53% is not drawn in the figure, and its n labels count images.

items.title: The error decomposition assigns causes by rule order; base rates explain most of the 15.5% 'definition' share and part of the 68% 'background' share
items.claim_affected: fig2b: "68% of CLIP's errors follow the background; the label definition explains 15% and the tern bug 3%"; Summary 2: "15.5% are water-tied landbirds (kingfishers, marsh birds) called waterbird"
items.argument: Rule 2 is checked before rule 3, so every error on a landbird rated ≥ 2 counts as 'definition', including errors the base rate would produce anyway. Rating-0 landbirds are wrong 53.0% of the time on water and 11.8% on land. The ≥ 2 landbirds have 301 water images and 287 land images, so even with no rating effect the rule would label about 159 + 34 ≈ 194 errors (11.4%) as 'definition'. The excess over that is only about 71 errors (~4%). The same applies the other way: in the conflicting groups, every error not called 'definition' is 'background' by construction. Yet CLIP already errs on 12.5% of landbirds on land backgrounds, so the background-attributable excess in landbird/water is about 956 errors, against 1,031 labelled. The strict-rule count (100 errors, 5.9%) is printed but appears in neither the figure nor the summary. Rule 2's waterbird clause can never fire, because all 43 dataset waterbirds are rated 3 (including Ring-billed Gull, whose reason says it forages on land). So 'definition' can only excuse landbird errors, by construction. The bars show each group's share of its own images, while the title is a share of all 1,706 errors, so the 68% cannot be read off the figure. The limitation text says the rule is not causal, but the headline still presents 15% as 'explained'.
items.suggested_check: Replace the priority rule with an excess-risk decomposition. Per background, the counterfactual for 'definition' is the rating-0 landbird error rate, and for 'background' it is the matched-background rate. Give species-clustered CIs. Put the range across rule orders and the strict rule (about 4-15% definition) in the fig2b title and in Summary 2. Draw a tick at the matched-background error rate on each conflicting-group bar. Either plot counts that add up to 1,706 or retitle with the per-group quantity. State in the caption that 'definition' can only apply to landbirds.

verification.title: The error decomposition assigns causes by rule order; base rates explain most of the 15.5% 'definition' share and part of the 68% 'background' share
verification.evidence: Recomputed: rating-0 landbird error rates are 53.0% on water and 11.8% on land. The ≥ 2 landbirds have 301 water and 287 land images, so base rates alone give 159.6 + 33.8 = 193.4 expected 'definition' errors (11.3% of 1,706). Observed is 264 (57 + 207), so the excess is only about 71 (~4%). In original-label landbird/water, the land-background error rate (12.5%) predicts about 281 of 2,255. The excess is 957, against 1,031 labelled 'background'. The cell-10 crosstab shows all 43 waterbirds rated 3, so rule 2's waterbird clause can never fire. The tern-bug species are rated 0 and are caught by rule 1. Ring-billed Gull is rated 3 with the reason 'though often forages on land'. The strict count (100) appears only in the cell-14 Finding, not in the fig2b title or Summary 2 ('15.5%'). Minor overstatements in the critique: fig2b prints segment counts, so 1,031 + 124 = 1,155 can be summed by hand. Cell 15's limitation says 'the decomposition is a rule, not a causal test', yet the title still says 'explains 15%'.

items.title: 'A small word beats a whole scene' compares different base images, doses and controls
items.section: §4 fig4b_dose_response title (cell 31), fig4d neutral control (cell 35), Finding 3, Summary 4
items.claim_affected: "the wrong word at 4% height ... fools 96.7% of landbirds and 78.3% of waterbirds; a conflicting scene behind a full-size bird fools 39.0% / 20.8%"; "flips 96.7% of landbirds"; "The neutral word 'triangle' (-0.13) shows that occlusion alone does little"
items.argument: The word is written on the original canvas, where half the landbirds already sit on a conflicting water background. Recomputed read-only: 32.3% of the sampled landbirds are wrong with no text at all. The scene number instead uses the cut-out bird at scale 1.0 (80% of the canvas), which is the scene's weakest dose; at scale 0.15 it fools 99%. 'Flips' also counts birds that were already wrong: among originally correct birds the rates are 95.1% and 76.0%. The neutral control is not negligible on the original base. The 4% 'triangle' box moves landbird errors from 32.3% to 19.2% and waterbird errors from 9.7% to 22.5%; in fig4b the dotted neutral-word curves shift the margin by about +0.7 and -1.5. 'Occlusion does little' therefore holds only on the gray base. The control is also a single word. The other meaningless string, 'xkqzvrtb', gives +0.90, and against that zero 'ocean' nets only +0.85 and 'lake' +0.47. Box size is not matched either: cue.overlay_text fixes the cap height, so box width follows the letters (up to about 2.4x in area between 'waterbird' and 'tree'), and the recorded text_box_area is never used. The direction survives in margin units, but the headline shares exaggerate the contrast and depend on an arbitrary pairing of doses.
items.suggested_check: Compare word and scene on a shared base and against their own controls (misleading minus neutral word; conflicting plate minus gray at the same scale). For example, extend 4d's gray-base design to several text sizes and bird scales. Report flip rates only among birds correct on the unedited canvas, split by original background. Add 10-20 neutral words, length-matched random strings and a blank white box. Report each word's Δ minus the matched-control mean, and regress word Δ on box area. Retitle fig4b to say the comparison holds only for the chosen doses.

verification.title: 'A small word beats a whole scene' compares different base images, doses and controls
verification.evidence: Recomputed from the cue cache. With no text, 32.3% of the sampled landbirds and 9.7% of the waterbirds are already wrong on the canvas (52.7% in landbird/water). The misleading 4% word gives 96.7% / 78.3% wrong overall and 95.1% / 76.0% among originally correct birds. The scene number in the fig4b title uses scale 1.0 (39.0% / 20.8%), but at scale 0.15 the conflicting plate fools 98.7% / 50.0%, so the contrast depends on the dose pairing. On the original base, the neutral 'triangle' box at 4% gives 19.2% landbird and 22.5% waterbird errors, and Δmargin ≈ +0.78 / -1.54 (dotted curves in fig4b). Among originally correct waterbirds it flips 14.2% (24.9% on land backgrounds). So 'occlusion alone does little' holds only on the gray base used in 4d. 'xkqzvrtb' is +0.90 in 4d, which leaves 'ocean' net +0.85 and 'lake' +0.47. Box areas at 8% differ by word: waterbird 4.1% vs. tree 1.8% (2.25x), and triangle 4.8%, xkqzvrtb 5.4%. Mitigating: fig4d already compares word and scene on one base (+4.81 vs. +1.49), and the strong scene words ('ocean' 2.2%, 'lake' 1.9%) have smaller boxes than the neutral control. Box area therefore cannot explain the word effects. The critique also concedes that the direction survives.

items.title: Section 5's error clusters and k-NN test do not beat trivial baselines (the group label; CLIP's own prediction)
items.section: §5 fig5_projection_clip_outputs, cluster table (cell 40), description checks (cells 48-49), fig5d_dinov2_comparison (cells 46-47), Summary 5
items.claim_affected: "5 stable clusters hold 79.5% of all errors in 51.2% of the images ... Each has a describable reason"; "Errors are neighbours in CLIP's output space (k-NN AUC 0.89) more than in an independent image space (0.80)"; "If they cluster only in CLIP's output space, the errors come from how CLIP reads the images"
items.argument: (a) Clusters are flagged against the overall 29.0% error rate, not against the rate expected from their group mix. From the printed compositions and the corrected group error rates (12.5 / 54.9 / 20.7 / 0.8%), C1 (86% landbird/water) should be about 49% wrong but is observed at 39.3% [34.9, 43.8]. So the 'bright yellow songbirds' region is protective, not an error region. The group label alone concentrates errors more than the clusters do: landbird/water holds about 1,264 of 1,680 errors (75%) in 40% of the images (lift 1.89), against 79.5% in 51.2% for the clusters (lift 1.55). (b) The descriptions are drafted and tested on the same data. The code is looser than the stated '2x' rule: 1.5x for C9, which passes at 1.78x, and a 0.9x median area for C3. assert checks.kept.all() leaves no room for a description to fail, and the named species sets for C9, C3 and C4 are never tested. (c) 'Error' is the sign of CLIP's own s compared with the label. The 230-d vector holds 200 species logits that nearly reproduce s (soft routing class AUC 0.96), plus scene prompts that include the Places categories behind Waterbirds. One reviewer re-ran the test. The k-NN AUC for CLIP's own prediction is 0.959 in CLIP-output space vs. 0.863 in DINOv2 space. Within waterbird/land, the error AUC is 0.69 vs. 0.72, so DINOv2 does better there. The 0.89 vs. 0.80 gap mostly restates that CLIP's outputs encode its own prediction. fig5d's bars start at 0.45, which exaggerates the gap, and no k-NN AUC has a CI.
items.suggested_check: Flag error clusters by observed vs. composition-expected error (indirect standardisation) with a CI, and retitle with the lift relative to the group baseline. In fig5c, contrast same-group members inside vs. outside a cluster. Fix one enrichment rule before running the checks. Draft descriptions on half the images and test them on the other half. For the k-NN test, report per space the AUC for CLIP's prediction and the within-group error AUCs. Recompute after regressing s out of each of the 230 columns, add bootstrap CIs, and plot dots on an axis starting at 0.5. Drop 'the errors come from how CLIP reads the images' unless the gap survives within groups.

verification.title: Section 5's error clusters and k-NN test do not beat trivial baselines (the group label; CLIP's own prediction)
verification.evidence: Reproduced the clustering exactly (cluster sizes, and 79.5% of errors in 51.2% of images). (a) Composition-expected error: C1 observed 39.3% vs. expected 49.0%, so C1 is protective. The other flagged clusters are above expectation: C9 59.3 vs. 48.6, C3 43.8 vs. 23.1, C4 39.7 vs. 25.1, C0 38.7 vs. 28.8. The group label alone puts 1,264 of 1,680 errors (75.2%) in 39.7% of images (lift 1.89), against 1.55 for the clusters. (b) Cell 49 uses `a/b >= 1.5` for C9 (passes at 1.78), while cell 48 states 2x. `assert checks.kept.all()` forces every description to pass. C9 and C3 are tested only on place and size, and C4 only on landbird error, so their named species sets are never tested, even though Summary 5 repeats them. (c) The k-NN AUC for CLIP's own prediction is 0.959 (CLIP outputs) vs. 0.863 (DINOv2). That gap matches the error gap (0.887 vs. 0.804). Fig5d uses `set_xlim(0.45, 1.02)` and shows no CIs. Caveats against the critique: the C3 0.9x median-area rule does not loosen the stated rule, which only asks for 'a smaller median bird'. The within-group comparison is selective: CLIP-output space beats DINOv2 in 3 of 4 groups (0.91 vs. 0.77, 0.84 vs. 0.75, 0.88 vs. 0.78), and DINOv2 wins only in waterbird/land (0.69 vs. 0.72). Within a group, error equals the prediction, so that test cannot remove the self-prediction confound anyway. Regressing s out of the 230 columns is the right control.

items.title: 'The bird wins because its evidence is larger' compares an idealised bird on gray with an inpainting-damaged background, and R² = 0.83 is mostly the 2x2 design
items.section: §4 masks and inpainting (fig4_qc_masks_random, fig4_qc_conditions), fig4a additive fit (cell 30), Finding 1, Summary 4
items.claim_affected: "When the two disagree, the bird wins 65.4% [61.6%, 69.3%] of the time, because the bird's evidence is usually larger in magnitude (mean |s| 3.03 ... vs. 1.97)"; "s(orig) ≈ 0.67·s(bird only) + 0.65·s(background only) (R² = 0.83)"; "about equally per unit of evidence"
items.argument: bird_only is an isolated bird on flat gray. bg_only is the scene with a Telea-inpainted, 9x9-dilated, bird-shaped smudge covering a median 16-18% and up to 60% of the canvas. This degradation is uneven: it shrinks |s(bg_only)| as the bird gets larger. That alone could produce 'bird evidence larger (3.03 vs. 1.97)' and 'bird wins most conflicts'. The limitation text mentions the smudge but not this bias. The clean-mask rule checks only geometry, and the random QC sheet shows clean masks that include a float with a person, a hiker, a boat and second birds. A quick read-only check suggests leakage is small on average: bird-only s differs by 0.03 between the two landbird groups and by 0.31 between the two waterbird groups, and bg-only s by about 0.1 between classes. The notebook never tests this, though. The R² is pooled over a balanced class x background design. The four group dummies alone give R² = 0.58, and fitted within each group the additive model reaches only 0.54-0.66. 'Equal per unit' compares the slopes of two regressors measured on different artificial inputs with different measurement error, and no equivalence margin is given.
items.suggested_check: Calibrate the inpainting smudge. Paste random masks from other images onto the 20 bird-free plates, inpaint them, and regress Δs against the clean plate on mask area. Re-run the 65.4% after dropping the largest-mask tercile, or after correcting s(bg_only) by that slope. Use the balanced test split as a leakage test: within a class, bird-only s should not differ by background, and within a background, bg-only s should not differ by class (report CIs). Report the group-dummy baseline and the within-group R², or fit with group fixed effects. Drop 'about equally per unit', or give a paired CI with an equivalence bound.

verification.title: 'The bird wins because its evidence is larger' compares an idealised bird on gray with an inpainting-damaged background, and R² = 0.83 is mostly the 2x2 design
verification.evidence: Confirmed: bird_only is the bird on flat gray, and bg_only uses cue.inpaint (9x9 dilation, Telea). Median mask area is 15.8-18.4% per group (cell 23), and the clean rule allows up to 60%. In fig4_qc_masks_random, green (clean) masks take in an inflatable float with a person, a hiker behind a tern, a boat under a gull, and second birds (Green Kingfisher/Gadwall, Rhinoceros Auklet). The leakage numbers match a read-only check of cue_v1_300.parquet: bird_only s is -2.59/-2.56 for landbirds and 2.89/3.20 for waterbirds; bg_only s is -1.03/-0.93 and 2.60/2.70. The R² critique also holds: group dummies alone give R² = 0.58. The additive fit within groups gives 0.59/0.66/0.54/0.61, and 0.60 with group fixed effects. Within-group slopes are 0.51-0.70 for the bird and 0.50-0.61 for the background, and there is no paired CI or equivalence bound for 0.67 vs 0.65. Not supported: the central bias mechanism. |s(bg_only)| does not shrink as the bird gets larger: it is 1.94/1.96/2.00 across the mask-area terciles, and Spearman rho(area, |s_bg|) = 0.03. So the 3.03 vs 1.97 gap does not come from the smudge growing with the bird. The share of conflicts that follow the bird does rise with area (59%/64%/72%), but dropping the largest tercile still leaves 62.0% (n = 371 conflicts), so 'the bird wins most conflicts' survives. The limitation in cell 37 mentions the smudge only in general terms.

items.title: Section 2's 'ecology' and section 5's 'appearance' explain overlapping errors, and neither controls for the other
items.section: §2 fig2a and decomposition vs. §5 C0/C4 profiles and descriptions (cells 44, 49), §3 routing list (cell 20), Summary 2 and 5
items.claim_affected: Section 2: errors on rated ≥ 2 landbirds are definition disagreements where "CLIP sided with the ecology"; Summary 5: "a third cue, bird appearance: all-black birds and kingfishers, large woodpeckers and ravens are read as waterbirds"
items.argument: 5 of the 15 landbirds rated 2 are black icterids or corvids: Red-winged, Rusty and Yellow-headed Blackbird, Boat-tailed Grackle and Fish Crow (checked in species_water_rating.csv). These are the same birds section 5 attributes to an appearance cue, and Pied Kingfisher is black-and-white. The appearance claim rests on the C0 regex, which also matches waterbird families (Cormorant, Albatross, Frigatebird), so the enrichment does not show that black landbirds are misread. C0's top scene prompts are 'dark photo of a bird' and 'black and white photo of a bird', so plumage is also confounded with dark or desaturated photos. C4's 'mean water rating 2.07' mostly reflects its class mix: it is 59.6% waterbirds, all rated 3. Its 281 landbirds (96.8% wrong) average about 0.69, so at most about 35% of them can be rated ≥ 2, and the ravens and woodpeckers named in the description are rated 0. Section 3's routing list agrees: 5 of the 8 landbird species most often routed to a water species are rated 0. So the rating explains only a minority of confident landbird→waterbird misreads, and the profile table suggests the opposite.
items.suggested_check: Tag landbird species by plumage (all-black / mostly black / other) and by median mask area. Tabulate the error rate by rating x plumage x background with species-clustered CIs, or fit a logistic model with a species random effect. Compare rated-0 black species (American Crow, Common Raven, cowbirds, Groove-billed Ani) with rated-2 black species. Use the cached bird_only margins to test black vs. non-black landbirds without any background. Report the C0/C4 rating distributions for landbirds only. In Summary 2/5, state what share of confident landbird→waterbird errors come from species rated ≥ 2.

verification.title: Section 2's 'ecology' and section 5's 'appearance' explain overlapping errors, and neither controls for the other
verification.evidence: species_water_rating.csv confirms that the rated-2 landbirds include Red-winged, Rusty and Yellow-headed Blackbird, Boat-tailed Grackle and Fish Crow. The C0 regex in cell 49 includes Cormorant|Albatross|Frigatebird, which match 7 waterbird species. C0's top scene prompts are 'dark photo of bird' and 'black and white photo of bird' (cell 44). For C4, 59.6% are waterbirds; the landbird mean rating works out to about 0.69, so at most about 35% of them can be rated >= 2. Both ravens and all the woodpeckers are rated 0. Five of the 8 species in cell 20's routing list are rated 0 (Great Grey Shrike, Pileated Woodpecker, Dark-eyed Junco, Brown Creeper, Rose-breasted Grosbeak). A read-only check on the cached logits goes further: only 17% of all landbird->waterbird errors, and 18-20% of the confident ones (s > 1 to s > 3), come from species rated >= 2. On land backgrounds, non-black rated-2 landbirds are wrong 5.1% of the time (n = 136), less than non-black rated-0 landbirds (11.0%). Black rated-0/1 species are wrong 25.3% (n = 95), black rated-2 species 16.2%, and rated-3 species (mostly kingfishers) 49.4%. So section 2's land-background gap (19.9% vs 11.8%) is carried by black plumage and kingfishers, not by the water tie itself. The notebook controls for neither.

items.title: Section 3 cannot separate the word from the image: background AUC rises whenever bird information falls, and every rewording adds habitat words
items.claim_affected: "The shortcut is not in the word 'waterbird'. Every descriptive rewording makes the background effect stronger (paired difference CIs all above 0)"; "Routing ... leaves the background effect where it was (-0.006 [-0.018, +0.006])"
items.argument: The background AUC ranks s within a class. It therefore measures the background shift relative to the spread within the class, and that spread is mostly bird evidence. A wording with less bird content ('lives on', class AUC 0.67) shrinks the spread, so the background AUC rises (0.918) even if the shift in logits stays the same. Species routing widens the spread, so an unchanged AUC there implies a larger absolute shift. In fig3 the background AUC rises exactly where the class AUC falls, which is what less bird information predicts. All three rewordings also add explicit habitat words ('seabird or waterfowl', 'gull, duck, pelican ... water bird', 'lives on water'). A stronger background effect is therefore expected from the text itself and does not show that the image is the problem. The limitation calls the AUC a rank measure but does not mention this coupling. 'Unchanged' for routing is an absence-of-difference claim with no equivalence margin, and its paired bootstrap resamples images although the routing score is species-driven. Panels b and c use different truncated ranges (b starts at about 0.79 despite its '0.5 = no effect' label), so the two shifts cannot be compared by eye.
items.suggested_check: Score the cached edited images (birds on gray, bird-free plates, paste_match/paste_conflict) with every prompt pair and with the routing score. Per strategy, report the background swing (conflicting minus matching plate, same bird and scale) divided by the bird swing (waterbird vs. landbird on gray). Add a habitat-free pair, e.g. 5 prototypical species names per class. Replace panels b and c with one scatter of background AUC vs. class AUC with 2-D CIs. Use a species-cluster paired bootstrap for d_bg, and state an equivalence bound before calling routing 'unchanged'.

verification.title: Section 3 cannot separate the word from the image: background AUC rises whenever bird information falls, and every rewording adds habitat words
verification.evidence: Confirmed: all three rewordings add habitat words ('land bird' / 'seabird or waterfowl', '... other land bird' / '... other water bird', 'lives on land/water'; cell 16 and the prompt bank). 'Routing leaves it unchanged' rests on a CI that includes 0, with no equivalence margin. The CIs are image-level bootstraps (cell 16). In fig3, panel b's x-axis starts at about 0.79 and panel c's at about 0.64, despite the '0.5 = no effect' label. Partly refuted: the AUC rise is not only a spread artifact. From the cached logits, the mean within-class background shift in raw logits grows for every rewording: 2.54 at baseline, 3.01 for habitat words, 5.62 for example taxa, 3.22 for lives on. The ratio of background shift to class shift grows as well: 0.65 to 0.87, 1.14 and 3.48. 'Example taxa' keeps almost the baseline class AUC (0.892 vs 0.910) yet shows the largest background-AUC rise (0.917), so the rise does not track the class-AUC fall 'exactly'. For routing, the raw shift is larger (3.18) but its ratio to the class shift is smaller (0.51), which fits the notebook's 'sharper bird evidence' reading. Section 4d also gives direct evidence on the image side: a real water plate moves s by +1.49 on the gray base.

items.title: Alternative mechanism: 'waterbird' may respond to plain, low-texture or dark inputs rather than to water
items.section: §4 Finding 2 (tiny bird on gray), fig4d ('xkqzvrtb'), fig4_qc_plates, §5 C0, Phase II question 3
items.claim_affected: "Even on plain gray, a tiny landbird gets a negative margin (mean -0.44 at scale 0.15): a small bird without context already leans 'waterbird'"; "the unreadable string 'xkqzvrtb' (+0.90) still pushes towards water, which we cannot explain"; "Water scenes pull harder than land scenes"
items.argument: The empty 128-gray canvas was never scored. At scale 0.15 (a 27 px bird), 'a small bird leans water' and 'the gray canvas leans water' therefore cannot be told apart. Several content-poor or atypical inputs all push towards 'waterbird': the tiny bird on gray, the nonsense string and the inpainting smudge. The water plates are mostly smooth, low-texture fields (pale beach, sky and surf, an almost uniform slope, mostly sky with a sailboat). All 10 land plates are dense bamboo or foliage. So 'water vs. land' is confounded with 'plain vs. cluttered'. Suppose 'a photo of a waterbird' simply matches a bird against any plain background, as seabirds against sky or sea would look. Then the same numbers follow without any water semantics, and the water-plate effect is inflated. C0's profile points the same way: its top prompts are 'dark photo of a bird' and 'black and white photo of a bird'.
items.suggested_check: Score content-free controls through the existing pipeline: the empty gray canvas, black and white fills, each plate's mean colour, and Gaussian noise. Score low-pass-blurred and phase-scrambled versions of the 20 plates, and compare land and water plates matched on texture energy. Add a few neutral plates that are neither land nor water (sky, urban, indoor) as a third reference. For the appearance cue, darken or grayscale non-black landbird images and measure Δs.

verification.title: Alternative mechanism: 'waterbird' may respond to plain, low-texture or dark inputs rather than to water
verification.evidence: Confirmed: no empty-gray, solid-fill or noise canvas appears among the conditions (cell 27 table, experiment.conditions). At scale 0.15, both classes lean water on gray (cached mean s: +0.44 for landbirds, +1.65 for waterbirds), so 'a small bird leans water' cannot be told apart from 'the gray canvas leans water'. The notebook only lists 'the gray canvas' as an open Phase II question (cell 58, Q3); it does not test it. All land plates are vegetation. Overstated: fig4_qc_plates shows only about 4 of the 10 water plates are smooth (pale beach, sky with a sailboat, uniform slope, sunset sea). The rest are textured: a crater lake with a rocky island, lily pads with stepping stones, breaking waves, tree reflections, dark water with a snowy branch. Per-plate Δs against the same bird on gray (cached cue scores): the strongest water pushes come from textured plates (waves +2.78, tree reflections +2.27). Smooth plates average +1.59 vs +1.30 for textured ones, and the cluttered land plates range from -2.95 to +0.03. So 'plain vs. cluttered' explains the water-plate effect poorly. The 'xkqzvrtb' (+0.90) and C0 'dark photo' observations remain unexplained.

items.title: Section 5 projects a 230-d linear readout of CLIP's image embedding, which a grader may count as projecting embeddings
items.section: §5 cells 38-44 (fig5, fig5b, fig5c), aivis/clipscore.py, the black-box statement in cell 0
items.claim_affected: "Each image is described by its output vector ... (230 numbers; no embeddings)"; intro: "No hidden states, attention, gradients or embedding vectors are analyzed, plotted or projected"
items.argument: Each logit is τ·⟨v̂, t̂_j⟩ for a fixed text direction t̂_j, and per-image centring and per-prompt z-scoring are affine maps. So X = M·v̂ + c with a fixed 230x512 matrix M. UMAP, PCA (30 PCs = 93.4% of the variance), k-means and k-NN all run on a linear sketch of the normalised image embedding, restricted to the span of 230 text directions. The notebook asserts compliance but never argues it. The Phase I rule forbids plotting or projecting CLIP embeddings. If a grader reads this as projection by proxy, all of section 5 and Summary 5 count as Phase II material.
items.suggested_check: Get an explicit OK from the instructor, and add a short paragraph arguing why prompt-logit vectors count as outputs. As a fallback, show that the error-cluster and C0/C4 findings survive on a few named, interpretable output scores: the 30 scene-prompt logits minus a reference prompt, plus the soft routing score.

verification.title: Section 5 projects a 230-d linear readout of CLIP's image embedding, which a grader may count as projecting embeddings
verification.evidence: The math is right. clipscore.logits returns logit_scale * v_hat @ t_hat.T, and cell 39 subtracts each image's mean and z-scores each prompt. So X is an affine function of v_hat, restricted to the span of the 230 text directions, and 30 PCs explain 93.4% of its variance (cell 40). Cells 0 and 38 assert 'no embeddings' without addressing this; the clipscore docstring only argues that the feature vectors are never stored. The consequence is speculative, though: the stated Phase I rule explicitly allows 'CLIP's output logits (image-text similarities for any image and prompt)', and section 5 uses nothing else. Whether this counts as projecting embeddings is a matter of interpretation, not a clear violation. Adding a justification paragraph, or getting the instructor's OK, is still a sensible precaution.

items.title: The AI water rating rests on inflated kappa, non-independent raters and a pending human check that is not blind
items.section: §2 method and reliability (cells 9-10), species_water_rating.csv, handcheck_instructions.md, Summary 2
items.claim_affected: "4 independent AI raters" with quadratic κ 0.96-0.99; "a blind human check of 40 species"; rule 2: "the label contradicts the species' ecology, and CLIP sided with the ecology"
items.argument: κ is inflated by easy, bimodal cases: 111 species rated 0 and 43 obvious waterbirds rated 3. On the 53 landbirds that any rater put at ≥ 1, exact agreement drops to 0.62-0.77. Only 15 landbirds are rated ≥ 2 by all four raters, against 24 by at least one, and Sonnet alone drops 5 species from the ≥ 2 set. Raters A and D are the same model (κ 0.992), and the adjudicator is Opus too. All 4 ties where A and D agreed against B and C went to the Opus side. Two of them sit exactly at the cut that decides set membership: Le Conte Sparrow (2-1-1-2 → 2) and Louisiana Waterthrush (3-2-2-3 → 3). The human check is not blind in practice: its instructions say the list contains 'all 20 landbird species the AI rated 2 or 3'. It covers only 6 of the 111 rated-0 landbirds, so it cannot find false negatives, it has no pass criterion, and Summary 2 reads the same whether it passes or fails. The raters saw only species names, and about 11 of the 20 high-rated landbirds have a water word in their name. The rating and CLIP may therefore share one web-text prior rather than CLIP 'knowing ecology'. The limitation text mentions shared training data but none of these specifics.
items.suggested_check: Re-run the fig2a contrasts and the decomposition with each single rater, and with the set of species all four raters put at ≥ 2. Report the range. Report κ on the binary ≥ 2 indicator over the 157 landbirds. Validate against a non-LLM trait source, e.g. AVONET Primary.Lifestyle / Habitat or the EltonTraits foraging strata. Have someone outside the pair (e.g. the human-only team) do the hand check on a shuffled list with 15-20 extra rated-0 landbirds. Decide in advance what happens if binary κ < 0.6. Until then, mark Summary 2 as provisional.

verification.title: The AI water rating rests on inflated kappa, non-independent raters and a pending human check that is not blind
verification.evidence: Confirmed from species_water_rating.csv: 111 species rated 0, and 43 waterbirds plus 5 landbirds rated 3. 15 landbirds are rated >= 2 by all four raters vs 24 by at least one. Rater B (Sonnet) puts 15 at >= 2 vs 20 in the final set; it drops Fish Crow, Mangrove Cuckoo, Le Conte Sparrow, Bank Swallow and Tree Swallow. A-D kappa is 0.992. All 4 splits where A and D agreed against B and C (Olive-sided Flycatcher, Le Conte Sparrow, Louisiana Waterthrush, Cedar Waxwing) went to the A/D value. handcheck_instructions.md says the list contains 'all 20 landbird species the AI rated 2 or 3', and it has only 6 rated-0 landbirds. Cells 10 and 57 set no pass criterion. About 13 of the 20 high-rated landbird names contain habitat words (Kingfisher, Waterthrush, Marsh, Seaside, Mangrove, Bank, ...). Exact agreement on the 53 landbirds that any rater put at >= 1 is 0.62-0.77; the critique's range leaves out A-D, which is 0.91. Overstated: on the decision-relevant binary >= 2 indicator over the 157 landbirds, Cohen's kappa is still 0.79-0.95 for every pair (A-B 0.79, B-C 0.81). So the critique's 'binary kappa < 0.6' contingency would not trigger, and rater disagreement at the cut is modest. The notebook also already runs a 'rated 3 only' sensitivity check (definition disagreements drop from 264 to 100), which makes the threshold dependence visible.

items.title: Reproducibility: cached results are not tied to their inputs, a cold run can break silently, and some numbers in the text come from no cell
items.claim_affected: "Every number in the text below is printed by an executed cell"; readme: "Delete the folder to recompute everything"; "Does our own implementation reproduce the known zero-shot behaviour"
items.argument: ex.run returns cue_v1_300.parquet whenever the file exists. Its cache key omits PLATE_PICK, SAMPLE, the masks, the prompts and the precision. ClipScorer defaults to fp16, and the bank cache was renamed *_fp32 but the cue cache was not. The plate is stored as a list position ('1-3'), so the cached scores cannot be checked against the plate list that changed at check-in 2. The executed section 4 was loaded from this cache. A cold run needs bit-identical rembg output to rebuild the 120 candidates; one flipped clean flag makes ranked.index(PLATE_PICK[...]) fail. Text rendering falls back to ImageFont.load_default(), which ignores the size. On a machine without Arial, all 8 text sizes would render the same and fig4b would break silently. Several numbers come from no cell: cell 25's '4 of the 10 land plates ... only 4 water images', and the rejected-attempt PNG (no SVG, older timestamp, titled '20 background plates'). Cell 51 says 'about a third' where the computed values are 0.20-0.33. The reproduction targets (.706/.876/.451/.749/.960) have no source and match to within 0.06 pp; if they came from an earlier run of this pipeline, the check is circular. The cell-28 QC figure draws plates with a fresh rng, so the plates shown are not the ones scored. check_equivalence covers only 16 images x 2 prompts. Dataset and model are loaded without revision=.
items.suggested_check: Store the plate image idx, SAMPLE and the precision in the cue parquet and assert them on load (or hash them into the file name). Commit the 20 plate crop boxes and SAMPLE as CSVs. Ship a TTF, load it by path and assert it is a FreeTypeFont. Pin revision= for the dataset and the model. Generate the rejected-attempt sheet in a cell or drop it, compute the 'third' in code, and cite the source of the expected accuracies. Take the cell-28 plates from the CUE 'plate' column. Then do one Restart & Run All with an empty AIVIS_CACHE, ideally on the human pair's machine, and diff every printed number.

verification.title: Reproducibility: cached results are not tied to their inputs, a cold run can break silently, and some numbers in the text come from no cell
verification.evidence: Confirmed: experiment.run returns cue_{name}.parquet whenever the file exists, and the key is only 'v1_300'. ClipScorer defaults to fp16=True. The plate column stores list positions ('1-3'). No revision= appears anywhere in aivis or the notebook. The expected accuracies in cell 5 have no source. Cell 25's '4 of the 10 land plates' and 'only 4 water images' are not computed by any cell. The rejected-attempt PNG has no SVG, is timestamped 19:33 (the other figures 20:58) and is titled '20 background plates' over 14 images. Cell 51 says 'about a third' where the values are 0.200-0.328, and check_equivalence covers only 16 images x 2 prompts. Refuted: the executed section 4 cache is not stale. The thumbnails cached together with the scores show exactly the current PLATE_PICK plates (pixel MSE 0 for 400 of 400 birds checked), and the cached s values are not on an fp16 grid, so they were computed in fp32. A changed candidate list in a cold run fails loudly at ranked.index or the assert in cell 26; it does not break silently. _font tries arialbd.ttf, then DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf, before load_default, so a machine without Arial is not enough to trigger the fallback. The two example birds in cell 28 (#93, #18) are not in the 1,200-bird sample, so no scored plate is shown wrongly.
